title: Prairie Avenue (looking North West) [west side, 1702–1812] — 'Views of Chicago', p. 233
camera_position: imaginary elevated viewpoint over the east side of Prairie Avenue between 17th and 18th Streets, looking across the roadway at the west-side house fronts from 1702 to 1812 (18th Street crossing mid-strip)
creator: Rand, McNally & Co. (artist unrecorded)
repository: Internet Archive (digitized from University of Illinois at Chicago Library)
collection: Lawrence J. Gutter Collection of Chicagoana (UIC); Rand, McNally & Co.'s bird's-eye views and guide to Chicago (1893)

notes: Left-hand of the two vertical strip drawings on printed page 233 (IA leaf n244; IIIF image _0245; crop x0–905 of the page). Block-by-block perspective line drawing with printed house numbers on the curb line: 1702, 1712, 1720, 1726, 1730, 1736, '18th St.', 1800 (Glessner, with its arched entry and 18th-Street wall), 1808, 1812. Shows uniform setbacks, front lawns, a continuous line of curbside posts/lamp-or-hitching posts and street trees, a carriage in the roadway. Drawn c.1892–93: 1702 here is the pre-Glessner-Lee-townhouse house (pa-1702-43, demolished before 1904) and 1726 is the early house later replaced, so for 1904 this is evidence of the earlier generation at those two lots; 1720, 1736, 1800–1812 are the buildings standing in 1904. Diagrammatic — façades are simplified and proportions not reliable for measurement; treat as a numbered sequence/massing guide.

title: Prairie and Michigan Avenues — Views of Chicago (Portland, Me.: L. H. Nelson Co., 1905)
addresses: Prairie Avenue and/or Michigan Avenue (blocks not identified)
camera_position: two sidewalk-level views along a residential avenue (left vignette: on the sidewalk between curb trees and house lawns, looking down the walk; right: on the sidewalk beside high-stoop row houses and a stone Gothic church) — which avenue and which block is not stated
creator: L. H. Nelson Company (publisher); photographers unrecorded
repository: Internet Archive (Library of Congress copy, Sloan Foundation scan)
collection: Views of Chicago (L. H. Nelson Co., 1905); IA item viewsofchicago00por
rights_basis: Published 1905 in the U.S.; IA possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT
found_via: archive.org full-text search 'Prairie' inside viewsofchicago00por (caption 'PRAIRIE AND MICHIGAN AVENUES'); same plate recurs in the 1908/1909/1910 editions (viewsofchicago01port, viewsofchicago00portl, viewsofchicago00portla)
notes: Halftone page with two photographs captioned jointly 'Prairie and Michigan avenues are the homes of more millionaires than any other two streets in the city, including such men as Marshall Field, Frank O. Lowden, the late Potter Palmer… Both streets are rather wide and very well-kept.' Neither photo is individually labelled, so neither can be placed on Prairie 16th–22nd with confidence. Valuable as period evidence of the residential street section c.1900–05: wide concrete/stone sidewalk set back behind a grass parkway with a single row of closely spaced elms; a row of dressed-stone CARRIAGE BLOCKS / curb stones along the parkway edge (left view); cast-iron lamp post on the parkway (right view); high stone stoops with iron railings and low iron fences; smooth light-coloured roadway (asphalt or macadam) with carriages. Lowden lived at 1912 Prairie, so the caption at least names the district's residents.

notes: Wide view with the corner itself in the foreground: smooth light-surfaced roadway sweeping round the corner (no block paving visible), concrete sidewalk with grass parkway and young trees, low stone coping wall with square piers around the Pullman lot, and east along 18th Street the long low arcaded outbuilding (stable/'palm-house' wing) and an open horizon toward the lake. Strong streetscape evidence for the 18th-Street frontage and corner treatment c.1898–1910. title: The Homes of Chicago. — Residences of Prominent Citizens on Prairie Avenue (The Land Owner, May 1874)
addresses: Prairie Avenue at 18th Street (street vignette, per Glessner House blog)
camera_position: composite sheet of nine vignettes; the top-centre vignette lettered PRAIRIE AVENUE is a street-level view along the avenue (direction not stated); the others are corner/oblique views of single houses
creator: Drawn by Louis Braunhold; engraved by J. M. Wing & Co.; The Land Owner (Chicago)
repository: Chicagology (chicagology.com) — secondary website reproduction; original holder not stated
rights_basis: Published 1874 (U.S.); faithful scan of a 2-D public-domain engraving reproduced on chicagology
found_via: WebSearch → chicagology.com/chicagostreets/prairieavenue/ (image list extracted from page HTML)
notes: Vignettes captioned Louis Wahl, Edson Keith (1906), A. A. Dewey, Dan'l M. Thompson (1936, with its tower — later Allerton), C. M. Henderson (1816), Geo. M. Pullman (1729, before the 1892 remodelling), Robert Law (1620?), Marshall Field (1905) and the street scene. Shows the 1870s streetscape: board/picket and ornamental iron fences on low copings, plank or flag sidewalks, gas lamp posts, young parkway trees, unpaved or block roadway with carriages. Thirty years before 1904 — use for persistence of lot treatments (fences, copings, lamp types), not for 1904 façades of rebuilt houses. Original journal holder not traced (lead: The Land Owner, 1869–1880s, CHM/Newberry runs). Same plate as a18-gh-landowner-1874-plate (Glessner House blog copy, link-only); this record carries the local full-sheet file. The Glessner House blog identifies the top-centre street vignette as 'Prairie Avenue looking southwest at 18th Street' (the pre-Glessner corner) — see a18-gh-landowner-1874-glessner-site; the vignette captioned 'Louis Wahl' is 2026 Prairie.

W.P.' water-pipe annotations on Prairie, Calumet and Indiana (and 36-in. main on Indiana/Calumet), 'Bridge' and 'Commerce' as old names of 20th and 21st Streets, 18th St. shown as '(Old)' with its jog, private park lots east of Calumet at 20th, the IC & Michigan Central right-of-way with breakwater and lake beyond, and the diagonal Calumet Ave. strip near 18th. Original atlas copy to locate (lead: Newberry / CHM / UIC copies of the Greeley-Carlson 'Atlas of the City of Chicago', 1891, vol. covering South Division).
